note: Kar Narpathu 12: dark clouds like oiled elephants rise on the right every day, a sight beyond doubt that he will come. Mullaippattu 4-5: the cloud drinks the cold sea and rises rightward (வலனேர்பு), just before the old women go out to seek an omen.
teaches: The idyll sets the rightward-rising cloud beside a separate omen rite, while the venba makes the cloud itself the omen 'beyond doubt', which shows the rising on the right read as a good sign for the absent man's return.

note: Akananuru 9 ends with the returning man asking whether his heart, which went ahead longing for her soft shoulders, has reached her; Kar Narpathu 19 has the man say his heart has gone the long road wanting her as companion.
teaches: Both returning heroes speak of a heart that outruns the chariot, so the figure belongs to the set speech of return; the long poem follows the heart into the house and to her touch, while the venba stops at its setting out.

note: 283 line 6 names the assembly hall of the Kosar (கோசர் அவைக்களத்தானும்); Akananuru 262 names the town-elder Kosar (ஊர்முது கோசர்) who blinded Anni Mignili's father.
teaches: Both poets know the Kosar as a body that sits in judgment, an institution in the puram fragment and the source of a borrowed story in the akam poem, so the Kosar's council was famous enough for an akam speaker to cite it as a known wrong.

note: Verse 7 gives the purpose of his journey as giving to seekers and destroying foes; verse 8 gives it as lasting fame in this earthly world.
teaches: Read in sequence, the friend's account of his motive moves from duties toward others to fame for himself while her proof stays the same rain-season sign, so the series varies the cause of absence and holds the cure fixed.

note: Kural 241 ranks the wealth of அருள் above the wealth of goods, which even the base possess; Paripadal 5.80-81 refuses பொருளும் பொன்னும் and asks அருளும் அன்பும் அறனும்.
teaches: The Kural makes the ranking a general maxim about kinds of wealth, and the Paripadal turns that same ranking into the content of a prayer, showing the ethical scale used as the measure of what to ask a god for.

note: The same line, எழுமுடி கெழீஇய திருஞெமர் அகலத்து, describes the king's chest in 14 line 11, where it is the shield of the worthy, and in 16 line 17, where it is the queen's longed-for bed.
teaches: The decade reuses one formula of the crowned chest for war and for love, so the turn in 16 to the waiting queen is built from the same praise language and makes the protector of the realm the cause of her loneliness.

note: Purananuru 55.1-2 (மலைப் பெருவில் பாம்புஞாண் ... ஒரு கணை ... மூவெயில்) and Paripadal 5.24-25 (நாகம் நாணா, மலை வில்லாக, மூவகை ஆர் எயில் ஓர் அழல்-அம்பின்) give the three-forts deed in the same parts: mountain bow, serpent string, one arrow; both also turn on Siva's forehead eye.
teaches: The same tripura formula serves a puram poet as the vehicle of counsel to a Pandya king and a devotional poet as the prelude to Murugan's birth, showing that Siva's deed was common stock usable for statecraft and worship alike in the Sangam period.

note: Both use an elephant who gives food to his mate on the road the man took; in Kalittokai 11 the woman concludes that such a forest will bring him back; in Akananuru 59 the friend sets the same care against the men who do not remember (உள்ளார்).
teaches: One image of animal care is made to argue both for and against the absent man's faithfulness, so the force of the iraicchi depends on the speaker's purpose, not on the creature.

note: Both tell of Cheralathan, ashamed of his back wound from the fight with Karikalan, sitting facing north to die; Purananuru 65 laments the king, Akananuru 55 turns to the noble men who died with him.
teaches: The akam poem keeps a detail the puram lament leaves out, the companions who followed the king into death, and uses it to measure a mother's wish that her life would follow her daughter.

note: Purananuru 2 likens Udhiyan Cheralathan's patience, counsel, strength, wrath and grace to the five great elements; Patitruppattu 14 tells his son, named in the decade's preface as Udhiyan Cheral's son, that he is as beyond measure as earth, water, wind and sky.
teaches: Father and son are both praised through the elements, which shows the element catalogue working as a Chera family formula, and the son's version moves the point from the elements' separate qualities to their shared immeasurability.

note: Kar Narpathu 9: the flowers speak many sweet words announcing his return. Akananuru 74: the heroine tells the friend she could hold firm on her many sweet words of reassurance (வன்புறை இன்சொல் நன்பல) were it not for the herders' flute at evening.
teaches: Akananuru 74 gives the heroine's answer that the Kar Narpathu never records: sweet words of comfort hold her only until the evening flute, so the reassurance the venbas repeat is shown elsewhere to fail at its own hour.

note: In Kalittokai 11 the woman infers that the man who saw a stag shade its doe will come home; in Akananuru 34 the man, having seen a stag feed and guard its doe, urges his charioteer home.
teaches: The woman's inference is borne out from the man's side in the other anthology: the creature's care on the road does turn the traveller homeward, so the iraicchi is a shared convention both lovers trust.

note: Naladiyar 17 says youth falls like fruit, so do not desire a woman for her eyes; Kalittokai 15 says wealth can be made any day but youth cannot be brought back, so do not leave her.
teaches: From the same fact that youth passes, the moralist counsels turning from desire and the love poet counsels holding fast to it, so the two books read the brevity of youth as a reason for opposite lives.

note: Kural 230 says death is the bitterest thing, yet sweet when one cannot give; in 165 the giver says a bard going away disappointed is worse than losing his country and gives his head.
teaches: The Kural's ranking of giving above life is a figure of speech in a couplet; 165 gives it a narrative in which a dispossessed chief literally prefers death to failing a bard, so the maxim had a heroic story behind it.

note: In Kalittokai 13 the man lists what the waste would do to her if she came; in 6 the woman answers such a list by asking for hardship as her companion.
teaches: Read together, the danger catalogue is a convention both lovers know how to answer: in 13 the friend discounts it as teasing, in 6 the woman turns it into the reason to go together, so the list deters no one.

note: The preface says the king carved his bow on the Himalaya and brought costly vessels with diamonds (அருவிலை நன்கலம் வயிரமொடு கொண்டு) to his old city and gave to others; Akananuru 127 recalls Cheralathan who drove off the sea, cut the kadamba, carved his bow on the Himalaya and heaped the foes' tribute of fine vessels with diamonds (நன்கலம் ... வயிரமொடு) at Maanthai, leaving it for the earth to eat.
teaches: The two record the same hoard with the same jewel list but different fates, given away in the preface and left buried in the akam poem, so an akam poet could cite a puram event precisely while turning its moral from royal giving to abandoned wealth, the wealth the lover will not linger for.

note: Kural 557 likens the king's lack of grace to the world's lack of rain; Kalittokai 10 likens the drought-dried waste to a world under a crooked-sceptred king whose men rob and kill.
teaches: The comparison runs both ways: the ethics book explains tyranny by drought and the love poet explains drought by tyranny, so the bond between bad rule and failed rain was common enough to be used as vehicle or as tenor.

note: Kural 1152 says that union, which once gave delight even at a glance, now carries the pain of fearing separation; Kalittokai 4 shows the woman reading his coming departure in caresses that exceed the usual.
teaches: The poem supplies the mechanism the couplet leaves out: the fear spoils union because his tenderness itself has become the sign of leaving, so the more he gives the surer she is he will go.

note: Patitruppattu 11 likens the Chera, who reached the sea and felled the enemy's guarded kadamba at the root (முழுமுதல் துமிய), to Murugan who cut down Sur at the root (சூருடை முழுமுதல் தடிந்த); Thirumurugatruppadai 45-60 tells the god's deed itself: he entered the cold sea and cut Sur at the root (சூர்முதல் தடிந்த), the mango at its trunk.
teaches: Thirumurugatruppadai shows that cutting the root in the sea was already the god's signature deed, so the Chera poet's repeated phrase is a claim that the king's sea raid re-enacted Murugan's myth, with the enemy's guardian tree standing in for Sur's tree.

note: Kural 55 says the wife who worships her husband commands rain; Kalittokai 16 calls the woman the chaste one who gives rain to the world in drought and says virtue will not let her pale.
teaches: The power the Kural states as a marvel works in the love poem as an argument: a woman who can bring rain cannot be left to waste, so the belief served to bind husbands as well as to praise wives.

note: Akananuru 85: the friend tells the heroine not to weep, since the rain now spreading is the season he named when he assured them 'வருதும் யாம்'. Kar Narpathu 1 quotes the same promise, வருதும், and asks 'will he not come?'
teaches: The promise is the same word in both, which shows the friend's argument as a fixed form, quote his 'we shall come' and point to the rain, with the older poem supplying the peacock calling its mate as the proof the four-line verse leaves out.

note: Kural 247 states that this world is not for those without wealth; Kalittokai 14 puts the like saying (காதலார் எவன் செய்ப பொருள் இல்லாதார்க்கு) in the mouths of strangers and rejects it.
teaches: A maxim the Kural states as fact is quoted in the love poem as hostile outsiders' talk, so the wealth maxim was public wisdom that akam speakers could set against love and refuse.

note: Kar Narpathu 4: the season is the medicine for her pallor. Kural 1265: the pallor of her soft shoulders will leave only after she has seen her husband with full eyes; on a plain reading the two disagree about what cures pasalai.
teaches: The friend claims the sign of his return heals the pallor and the Kural's woman holds that only the sight of him will, so the couplet reads as the heroine's answer to the whole method of the Kar Narpathu's friend.

note: Both close on the failure of rain: 18 says Cheralathan will not lie even if rain fails for many years (மன்உயிர் அழிய யாண்டுபல துளக்கி ... தண்இயல் எழிலி தலையாது மாறி); 20 repeats the lines for the drought (மன்உயிர் அழிய யாண்டுபல மாறித் தண்இயல் எழிலி தலையா(து) ஆயினும்) and adds that he will not let a belly go hungry.
teaches: The repeated lines show that the decade has a fixed formula for drought, and 20 turns the general promise of 18 into a concrete guarantee against hunger, ending in a blessing on the mother who bore the giver.

note: Both have a mother figure following an eloped girl and asking those on the road whether they saw her: in Akananuru 7 the foster mother asks a doe and a hill girl; in Kalittokai 9 the mother asks brahmin ascetics, who answer.
teaches: The Akananuru leaves the question unanswered on the empty road, while the Kalittokai brings in renouncers to answer it with a doctrine, so the later anthology turns the mother's lament into a debate the elopement wins.

note: Kar Narpathu 5: he left fearing the words of those who scorn. Akananuru 111: the friend says he will come back, ashamed of the mocking words of hostile men (ஏஎச்சொல் நாணி).
teaches: Taken together, other men's contempt both sends the hero away for wealth and, in the friend's argument, drives him home again, so shame works on him at both ends of the journey.

note: Paripadal 5.1-4 (பனிக் கடல் ... புக்கு ... சூர் மா முதல் தடிந்து) and Thirumurugatruppadai 45-46 and 60 (பனிக்கடல் கலங்கவுள் புக்குச் சூர்முதல் தடிந்த ... மாமுதல் தடிந்த) tell the Sur deed in nearly the same words.
teaches: The near-identical phrasing in two different collections shows the Sur killing already had a fixed verbal formula, a shared stock of Murugan praise that both poets drew on rather than one poem borrowing a picture from the other.

note: Both say death comes unseen and no one knows the last day; the Naladiyar concludes that one must lay up provisions of virtue in time, Kalittokai 12 that one must not let the days of embrace pass for wealth.
teaches: The same reminder of death is used to opposite ends: the Jain moralist spends the uncertain time on merit, the love poet on love, so the memento mori did not belong to renunciation alone.

note: Kural 1263: she lives on, longing for the return of the man who went desiring victory with his resolve as his only companion. Kar Narpathu 7: the friend says he went to give to seekers and crush foes, and the rain will bring him back.
teaches: The couplet's woman treats his heroic aim as the rival that left her behind, while the friend names the same aim, giving and conquest, as a reason to trust he will return in the rains: one motive is a grievance in the Kural and a guarantee in the venba.

note: Kural 211 makes the rain the model of giving that seeks no return; Patitruppattu 18 says that even if the rain-cloud fails for many years, Cheralathan will not fail the bards' hope.
teaches: The Kural treats rain as the standard for duty-bound giving, but the Chera poem ranks the king above that standard because rain can fail, so the bards' praise claims for a patron a reliability the ethics book grants only to nature.

note: Kalittokai 2 calls the wife's chastity bright as the northern star (வடமீன் போல்) and sets her shoulders above wealth for suppliants; Purananuru 122 says Kari gives his land to brahmins and his tribute to bards and keeps as his own only the shoulders of his wife chaste as the northern star (வடமீன் புரையுங் கற்பின்).
teaches: The puram poem shows the patron's answer to the dilemma the akam friend poses: a giver can give everything away and still keep the wife's shoulders as his only possession, so generosity and staying home need not be traded off as the man in Kalittokai 2 supposes.

note: In Akananuru 51 the man tells his heart that wealth won by parting is not worth having and he will stay and hold her; in Kalittokai 18 the woman tells him the same and adds that even sharing one cloth, the united live the only true life.
teaches: The case against the wealth journey is made from both sides, and the woman's version goes further by accepting poverty outright, which the man's version never has to face.

note: Paripadal 5 asks Murugan for love (அன்பும்) instead of wealth; Thiruppugazh 986 asks for love growing ever greater, with tears, melting and faltering speech, and only then for the stainless meaning.
teaches: The Sangam prayer names love as one of three ethical gifts, while the Thiruppugazh makes love itself the whole request and describes its bodily signs, so the pair traces anbu changing from a virtue asked for into the felt experience of bhakti.

note: Kural 586 counsels the king to use spies who go in the guise of renunciants and wanderers; 47 insists that the bard's wandering life, crossing many wastes from patron to patron, harms no one. On the reading that 47 answers a suspicion of the wandering bard, the two disagree about whether such travellers should be trusted.
teaches: The Kural's advice to disguise spies as wanderers is the very reason a real wanderer could fall under suspicion, and 47 gives the wanderer's side, a life of gifts and honour that 'knows no harm to others', so the pair shows the cost the state's craft laid on the travelling poet.

note: In Akananuru 263 the mother says that had she known her daughter's mind she would have married her to the youth; in Kalittokai 9 the ascetics tell the mother that following the chosen man is the way of virtue.
teaches: What the Akananuru mother reaches only as regret, the Kalittokai states as a principle from outside the family: the girl's choice is rightful, so both books grant the eloping daughter the moral case against her parents.

note: Akananuru 44: the king has finished his work, the enemy has paid tribute, and the man bids the charioteer drive ahead to sleep on his wife's breast. Kar Narpathu 20: the glorious king's work is done, the roads are pleasant, and the rain moves like an army.
teaches: Both make the king's finished war the condition of the husband's return, and the pair shows the venba compressing the long poem's catalogue of kings and battles into one simile in which the rain-cloud marches like the armies he leaves.

note: Kalittokai 1 names three of Shiva's dances (kodukotti, pandarangam, kapalam); Tirumanthiram 2733 lists kodukotti and pandarangam among the dances whose king he is and places them in the nadis and at Tillai.
teaches: The dance names the Tirumanthiram files into a yogic doctrine were already in the oldest love anthology as stage dances with a partner keeping time, so the later mystic list inherited a performance repertoire, not a private vision.

note: Mullaippattu 1-6 likens the rain-cloud rising from the sea to Mal, who grew to measure the world; Kar Narpathu 1 likens the rainbow to the garland on the chest of Mal, coloured like the warring sea.
teaches: Both mullai poems open their rains with Mal, the god of the mullai land, so the land's god is the first image of its season; the later venba moves him from the rising cloud to the rainbow, making the sky his adorned chest rather than his growing body.

note: Akananuru 134: the returning hero tells the charioteer that if she hears the sound of the swift-horsed chariot (கடுமான் தேர்ஒலி) there may be union at midnight. Kar Narpathu 10: the friend hears the swift-horsed chariot coming like a forest stream and says the heroine will bloom.
teaches: The chariot's sound is the hinge of the reunion from both sides: the hero hopes she will hear it and the friend reports that it is heard and what it does to the heroine's body, in the same phrase கடுமான் தேர்.

note: Paripadal 5 has six of the seven sages' wives bear him; Thiruppugazh 372 names him the six-faced one who drank at the breasts of the six (அறுவர் முலையுணு).
teaches: In the Paripadal the six are mothers by conception through the fire, while in the Thiruppugazh they have become nurses he drank from, so the pair shows the six mothers' role shifting from bearing to nursing as the Krittika story settled.

note: Kural 333 says wealth does not stay, so do at once what does; Kalittokai 8 says wealth is less stable than a lute, Fortune or a cruel king, so do not go after it.
teaches: From the same premise the two draw different conclusions: the Kural says to spend unstable wealth on lasting good, the love poem says not to leave love to seek it, so impermanence argued for staying home as well as for giving.

note: In both the man leaves because he cannot refuse those who ask; in Akananuru 53 the wife says this means he loves wealth more than her and rejects the friend's calling it grace; in Kalittokai 2 the friend herself argues that such leaving is not love and wins.
teaches: The same honourable motive is judged in opposite directions by the same two persons in different poems: the friend excuses it in one and refutes it in the other, so the giving motive was a debated case in akam, not a settled virtue.

note: 16 asks whether the queen's bed will escape loneliness while the king lingers in camp; 19 says his love of war leaves no grace even for his modest wife, who has him only in dreams on the rare night he sleeps.
teaches: Taken together, the two poems show the decade returning to the queen's cost of war as a counter-voice inside praise, and 19 sharpens the question of 16 into a charge, set beside the ruin of the enemy's farmers.

note: Paripadal 5.9 names the split hill only by its crane name (குருகொடு பெயர் பெற்ற மால் வரை); Thiruppugazh 38 names it க்ரவுஞ்சம் and has it split together with the drying of the sea.
teaches: The Sangam poet renders the Sanskrit name Krauncha by its Tamil meaning, a hill named with the crane, while Arunagirinathar uses the Sanskrit name outright, so the pair shows the same deed passing from a translated to a borrowed name across a thousand years.

note: Akananuru 242 calls the velan who holds the veri rite ignorant (அறியா வேலன்): he blames the god for what is love; Paripadal 5.15-17 says the velan's praise and veri are neither true nor false, since the world lies within the god's bound.
teaches: Read together, the pair shows that the akam mockery of the velan was not a rejection of Murugan: the devotional poet keeps the rite valid at the level of the god while conceding that its particular verdicts may miss, which is exactly the room the akam friend exploits.

note: Both are reports of having seen the enemy's ruined land (கண்டனென் in Purananuru 23, கண்டுவந் திசினே in Patitruppattu 15), and both mark the ruin by white velai flowers growing over it (வேளை வெண்பூ; வெண்பூ வேளை).
teaches: The shared white velai shows it was a stock sign of a razed settlement in both Pandya and Chera praise, and Patitruppattu 15 extends the form: where Purananuru 23 ends on the waste, the Chera poet adds a second sight, the king's own guarded land, so the ruin becomes one half of a judgment on rule.

note: Purananuru 117 says Pari's land kept its rain even when Venus ran to the south and other evil signs appeared; Patitruppattu 13 says that in the king's guarded land Venus does not run into the burning quarter and rain stands where it is wanted.
teaches: Read together, the two show two views of the omen: the lament makes a just ruler's land immune to the bad sign, while the Chera praise has the good ruler prevent the sign itself, so royal virtue was imagined as reaching even the planets' course.

note: In Mullaippattu the old women seeking an omen hear a herd girl tell the calves 'இன்னே வருகுவர் தாயர்' and take it as a sign; in Kar Narpathu 2 the lightning speaks his message, 'இன்னே வருவர் நமர்'.
teaches: The same formula of reassurance, 'they will come at once', is an overheard chance word in the idyll's omen rite and the sky's own message in the venba, so the later poem turns the ritual of listening for a sign into the season speaking for the absent man.

note: Both anthology invocations show Shiva by his marks with the goddess beside him: Akananuru 0 sets Umai at his side on the bull; Kalittokai 1 has her keep the beat, measure and rhythm while he dances.
teaches: Each love anthology gives the god a partner suited to its form: the Akananuru, a book of spoken poems, seats her beside him, while the sung Kalittokai makes her the one who keeps time for his dance, so the consort's role follows the anthology's metre.

note: Kural 113 says to give up at once gain made by leaving fairness, even if it brings good; Kalittokai 14 says wealth made by leaving the straight way is an enemy in this life and the next.
teaches: The Kural allows that unfair gain may bring good and asks for sacrifice anyway, while the love poem denies it brings good in either world, so the woman's argument is stronger than the ethics book's rule.

note: 76 opens: killing and being killed is not new (புதுவது அன்று), it is the way of the world; 192 says dying is not new (சாதலும் புதுவது அன்றே).
teaches: The same commonplace serves opposite ends: in 192 the oldness of death leads to calm toward great and small alike, while in 76 it is granted only so that one king's feat can stand out as the thing never heard of before.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai 151-154 shows Siva only as one of three lords who come to see Murugan, with Uma, three unwinking eyes and the three forts destroyed; Paripadal 5.22-47 tells how that same god's union with Uma led to Murugan's birth.
teaches: The guide poem gives the kinship only as epithets (son of the god of the banyan, line 256) and shows Siva as a visiting lord, while the Paripadal narrates the birth in full, so the pair shows the story was known to both but told only where a poem chose to narrate rather than to direct a pilgrim.

note: Both liken the woman's fragrance to the kaanthal flowers of Nalli's hill slopes.
teaches: Nalli's hill and its kaanthal were a fixed image for a woman's scent, so a patron's country lent its fame to the beloved's body in more than one poet's hands.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai 253-255 (நெடும்பெருஞ் சிமையத்து நீலப் பைஞ்சுனை ... அறுவர் பயந்த) and Paripadal 5.48-49 (இமயத்து நீலப் பைஞ் சுனைப் பயந்தோர்) set the birth in the same blue pool and give him six mothers.
teaches: Both poems use நீலப் பைஞ்சுனை and the six who bore him, but only the Paripadal says who the six were and why their chastity stayed whole, so the guide poem's single epithet is seen to presuppose a full birth story its hearers already knew.

note: In Akananuru 5 the man says he gave up the journey because of his wife's silent, tearful sign; in Kalittokai 17 the friend says her own words, like medicine, made him give it up.
teaches: The same outcome is credited to whoever speaks the poem, the husband to the wife's mute grief and the friend to her own argument, so the given-up journey is a shared ending each voice claims.

note: Both liken the opening kodal cluster to a snake's raised hood in the rain-fed woodland; in Akananuru 154 the returning man sees it from the chariot, in Kar Narpathu 11 the friend points to it as the sign of his quick return.
teaches: The same flower-image is seen by the man on the road home and offered by the friend at home as a promise, so the shared stock of mullai images lets the two halves of a separation read the same sign in the same season.

note: Thirumurugatruppadai ends with the god giving the suppliant a rare gift (பெறலரும் பரிசில்) that makes him stand alone in the world; Paripadal 5.79-81 says we ask not wealth, gold or pleasure but grace, love and aram.
teaches: The guide poem frames devotion in the bard's economy of gifts, while the Paripadal explicitly refuses material gifts, so the pair shows two Sangam answers to what one should ask of Murugan, the patron's reward and the ethical state.

note: Kural 81 says the whole of living at home and guarding one's goods is for feeding guests; Kalittokai 8 ends that living in one's own house, protected by the king and tending guests, is itself wealth.
teaches: The friend turns the Kural's account of what wealth is for into an argument against the wealth journey: if a household already feeds its guests, it already has what wealth exists to buy.

note: Kural 1268: let the king fight and win; let us join the house and keep the evening feast. Kar Narpathu 20: the king's work is finished, so the roads home are sweet.
teaches: The couplet is the wish spoken while the war goes on and the venba is the same man once it is granted, so read together they give the before and after of one situation, the hero held by the king's war until it ends.

note: Kural 734 defines a land as one free of crushing hunger, unceasing disease and destructive foes; Patitruppattu 13 ends that the land the king guards has flowered, rid of disease and hunger (நோயொடு பசி இகந்து), after showing the enemy lands he ruined.
teaches: The Kural states the absences that make a land; the Chera poem shows who secures them and at whose cost, since the same king's anger is the destructive foe of his neighbours, so the definition is met at home by being broken next door.

note: Both carry the same thurai, the friend showing the season to reassure the heroine, with the konrai in bloom; Akananuru 4 ends with his chariot in sight, Kar Narpathu 4 with the season as medicine for her pallor.
teaches: Set together they give two endings to one speech: the long poem can produce the man himself on the horizon, while the four-line venba has to stop at the season and so makes the season itself the cure.

note: Patitruppattu 17 says the king's great victory drum was made from the kadamba he cut after driving back the sea (கடம்பு அறுத்து இயற்றிய வலம்படு வியன்பணை); in Akananuru 347 the heroine compares the street's gossip to the drum of Cheralathan who drove back the sea and cut the kadamba (கடம்பு அறுத்து இயற்றிய பண்ணமை முரசின்).
teaches: The near-identical wording shows an akam poet borrowing the Chera's victory drum, a puram fact, to measure how loud gossip is, so the king's war trophy had become familiar enough to serve as a household simile for noise.

note: Kural 1151: if you are not leaving, tell me; tell your quick return to those who will still be alive. Kalittokai 5 ends: whatever day you go, on that day her life will go.
teaches: Both refuse the comfort of a promised return by tying her death to the moment of departure, and the Kalittokai shows the couplet's sharp line as the close of a full argument, after images of the emptied festival ground and the lotus out of water have prepared it.

note: Purananuru 20 says that even if one could measure the sea's depth, the earth's breadth, the wind's paths and the sky, the Chera's knowledge, compassion and kindness could not be measured; Patitruppattu 14 says the king is as immeasurable as earth, water, wind and sky.
teaches: One poet makes the elements measurable so that the king can exceed them, the other makes them the standard of the unmeasurable, which shows that the same four-part catalogue could rank a king either above nature or alongside it.

iraicchi.act: the tusker feeds his mate the little muddy water first and drinks after her
iraicchi.sense: the man who saw such care on his road will keep faith and come back to care for her
